# v1.1 concept: fixed solid heat stores, regenerated by coolant during coast

Status: agreed architectural direction for investigation, **not implemented or
credited in the frozen v1.0.1 payoff**. First complete the staged-model workflow.
This supersedes the earlier v1.1 assumption that flowing liquid must carry most
of the dive heat immediately into a large hot coolant reservoir.

## The revised thermal cycle

Retain the useful function of the solid racks: cold solid surface accepts intense
gas heat during the short collection interval. Embed small coolant passages in
fixed, thermally conductive plates, fins or other gas-contact structures. During
coast, circulate coolant through those passages and an external radiator to
restore the solid's temperature distribution. Add a heat pump only if the chosen
cold endpoint requires one and its total mass/energy cost is justified.

The solid is the principal short-duration heat store. The coolant circuit is
primarily its recovery path, sized for the coast interval rather than automatically
for the peak atmospheric heat rate. Coolant circulation during collection is an
option, not a requirement for carrying the whole pass heat. No coolant is mixed
into the gas by this architecture; the independently supported mixing option remains.

The gas-contact structure no longer has to transform into a large radiating sheet.
It can stay mechanically supported inside the vessel, with separate choices for
solid inventory, gas passage geometry and embedded channel layout. Solar arrays
and external coolant radiators still deploy. Fixed pipe penetrations, valves,
expansion accommodation and service interfaces remain pressure-boundary hardware;
removing extraction hatches does not remove every seal or valve.

Apply this first to the higher-pressure volumes, including the main receiver.
The front SiC cooler is an **open decision**: compare retained direct deployment
through the mouth against a fixed solid store with a compatible recovery circuit.
Do not assume that every stage can use the same fluid or temperature circuit.
SiC is a ceramic; its joints, channel construction and thermal stress differ from
those of the downstream aluminum inventory.

## Why the main receiver motivates the change

In v1.0.1, the fifth rack cools gas after the last dive compressor, improving
storage density during filling. It remains trapped inside the pressurized receiver
until its scheduled +72-minute extraction. The new recovery path can remove heat
through sealed coolant passages **while the receiver remains pressurized** once
external heat rejection becomes available. It need not wait for tank emptying.
That may also support continued densification or reduce processing inlet enthalpy.
These are coupled effects to measure, not independent mass credits to add together.

The receiver offers much more room to distribute heat-transfer surfaces than an
upstream compressor inlet. It is still a finite-volume vessel: solid, coolant and
supports displace gas. A large tank cross-section can reduce velocities, but jets,
baffles, narrow passages and inlet/outlet routing can create high local velocities
or bypass. A high gas density helps at a given mass flux; density alone does not
establish negligible pressure loss or nearly perfect gas-to-solid exchange.

Put cold surface where the incoming gas can reach it during filling. A coil only
near the coast-processing outlet may miss the hot incoming jet. Distributed fins,
flow distributors or a controlled inlet path should be compared before crediting
uniform tank mixing. A large unused surface in a stagnant corner is not effective
surface merely because the model knows its area.

## Two different conduction distances

Three processes must be resolved separately:

1. Gas-to-surface exchange during the pass: finite area, local velocity, residence
   time, boundary layers, bypass and pressure loss.
2. Surface-to-solid heat spreading during the pass: how much of the nominal solid
   inventory can actually absorb heat before collection ends.
3. Solid-to-channel recovery during coast: channel spacing, conduction/contact
   resistance, coolant flow, radiator performance and the next starting state.

A screening scale is `diffusion distance ~ sqrt(alpha * time)`, with
`alpha = conductivity / (density * specific heat)`. It is a scale estimate, not
an exact allowable thickness or an exchanger-performance correlation. The longer
coast can permit wider channel spacing than a continuously cooled exchanger.
But a thick lump that cannot absorb heat through its exposed surfaces during the
minute-long pass cannot have its whole mass credited as usable storage merely
because it can be cooled over an hour. Distributed gas surfaces and embedded
channels solve different distance constraints.

For the same stored energy Q, the indicative rates are Q / collection time and
Q / available recovery time. The latter can be much smaller; actual recovery time
must exclude stowing/deployment, low temperature approach and unavailable power.
No heat is eliminated. The plant must reject the cycle's energy plus pump work
and, where used, heat-pump electrical input.

## Minimum useful reduced model

Begin with ordinary sensible solid storage, not PCM. Use a surface and interior
solid state per module (more nodes if needed), finite coolant-channel conductance,
and gas states consistent with the staged model. A lumped-solid approximation is
acceptable only after verifying gradients for the proposed geometry.

An energy bookkeeping template is:

- `dU_solid/dt = Q_gas_to_solid - Q_solid_to_coolant`
- `dU_coolant/dt = sum(Q_solid_to_coolant) + pump_heat - Q_rejected`

Separate radiator/heat-pump states where present; include inlet/outlet enthalpy
for circulating components. Keep gas-side heat removal equal and opposite to
solid input. Restore the solid **temperature distribution**, coolant energy and
inventory, and electrical states across the orbit. Do not use an unexplained
cooldown clamp or a single blended temperature to hide a hot core.

Internal design quantities include gas-surface geometry and solid mass, channel
radius/wall/spacing, module size, manifolds, coolant flow/control, coolant inventory,
radiator area and temperature band. Distinguish these from externally selected
craft diameter and current L/D. Reserve partition is an unresolved internal sizing quantity; see [draft 04](../local-issue-drafts/04-size-the-valve-only-reserve-from-the-burn-and-refill-schedule.md).

## System-level trades to retain

- **Heat rejection temperature:** hot recovery is radiatively efficient; the cold
  end has less temperature difference to drive transfer and weaker radiation.
  Different temperature loops or staged recovery may beat one common loop. A heat
  pump can improve cold-end recovery but adds work and rejected heat. Ammonia is a
  candidate for appropriate downstream temperatures, not a universal front coolant.
- **Tube size is not the only channel limit:** smaller passages trade thermal reach
  against pressure drop, pump power, manifolding, wall strength, blockage tolerance
  and manufacturability. Charge headers and joints, not just capillary bore volume.
- **Stationary fluid still sees the hot solid:** a pump-off interval does not insulate
  coolant inside its channels. Model its temperature, phase and pressure, or explicitly
  design isolation/drainback. Do not grant free survival of trapped cold liquid.
- **Mass accounting:** retain the solid thermal mass; remove only obsolete extraction
  mechanisms/doors. Add channels, supports, coolant, plumbing, pumps, insulation and
  dedicated radiator/storage hardware, net of genuinely shared systems. Do not assume
  a separate one-pass coolant reservoir is still needed at its old size.
- **Volume and mechanics:** distributed fixed structures may be easier to support,
  but expansion, cyclic thermal stress, vibration and access still constrain them.
  Metal/coolant displacement reduces receiver gas capacity and affects matched altitude.
- **Thermal integration:** share infrastructure where temperature levels permit.
  Compressor/propulsion heat is a real additional load; mixing a hot stream into
  the cold recovery circuit can destroy its useful temperature difference.
- **Gas and propulsion coupling:** early receiver cooling changes pressure and valve
  exchange with the reserve. Include feed availability and refill timing; do not
  count density improvement without its effect on the connected gas inventories.

## Comparison boundary

The meaningful comparison is between deployable solid storage, fixed downstream
stores with a deployable SiC front, and fixed stores throughout. All require the
same mission and gas-path accounting. Reduced deployment complexity alone does
not establish a payoff benefit. The proposed comparison protocol is in
[draft 15](../local-issue-drafts/15-develop-v1-1-fixed-solid-heat-stores-with-coast-coolant-recovery.md).

## Background, not validation of this design

NASA's [thermal-control review](https://www.nasa.gov/smallsat-institute/sst-soa/thermal-control/)
describes thermal storage for repeated/transient heat loads and fluid/heat-pipe
paths to heat sinks or radiators. It supports the general separation of storage
and transport; it does not establish atmospheric-scoop performance or the proposed
solid geometry. DOE's [thermal-storage overview](https://netl.doe.gov/sites/default/files/2021-02/Thermal_Energy_Storage_1Pager.pdf)
distinguishes sensible storage from latent storage. This proposal initially uses
the former; embedded channels do not make it a PCM design.
